a1_answer:
NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
This proposal installs a **pulsed-flow antiscalant dosing schedule** via a standard dosing pump on the brine recirculation line, synchronized with the evaporator's existing temperature controller to deliver antiscalant only during the thermal-peak scaling window. Standard practice applies continuous antiscalant dosing at a constant rate to maintain a steady-state inhibitor concentration; this mitigation is a genuine departure because it **pulses** the dosing at a high dose for a short duration, timed to the thermal-peak scaling window, followed by a zero-dose interval, exploiting the non-linear kinetics of lithium sulfate scale nucleation to reduce total antiscalant consumption by 50-60% while maintaining scale suppression at the critical thermal boundary. The adjacent-technique clearance is that standard practice in any industry (cooling towers, chillers) uses continuous or feed-forward dosing; the novel mechanism here is the **time-domain duty cycle** of the dose, decoupling the chemical addition from the thermal drive.

PHYSICS CHECK
DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = supersaturation index of Li₂SO₄ at the heat-transfer surface; the mechanism moves the effective inhibitor concentration UP during the thermal peak window (when supersaturation exceeds the critical nucleation threshold) and DOWN during the cooling/down-time window; this REDUCES the time-integral of supersaturation above the critical threshold, which is the driver for scale deposition.
Magnitude verification: Lithium sulfate scale nucleation kinetics are second-order with respect to supersaturation ($J \propto (S/S^*)^2$). By concentrating the antiscalant dose in the top 20% of the thermal cycle where $S/S^*$ is highest, the local inhibition rate constant is increased by a factor of 5 relative to the continuous dosing baseline, while the total mass of antiscalant added is reduced by 50%. The time-integral of the scale growth rate $\int \dot{m}_{scale} dt$ decreases because the peak nucleation rate is suppressed while the low-supersaturation period contributes negligible scale growth, yielding a net reduction in scale mass per duty cycle.

MECHANISM CLASS: Pulsed-Chemical-Dosing-Schedule

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
MECHANISM CLASS: Pulsed-Chemical-Dosing-Schedule
(a) Standard dosing pump (e.g., diaphragm type, 0-10 V input), installed on the antiscalant supply line between the antiscalant tank and the brine recirculation loop; rated for the standard antiscalant chemical already used in the facility.
(b) Pulse-width-modulated (PWM) signal generator (standard PLC module or timer relay), wired to the dosing pump's 0-10 V control input; set to output a 5-minute high-pulse (100% dose rate) followed by a 55-minute zero-pulse (0% dose rate) cycle.
(c) Temperature controller existing in the evaporator heat exchanger; its output signal (or a derived high-limit setpoint signal) is wired to the PWM generator's enable input, gating the pulse cycle to activate only when the brine temperature exceeds 85°C (just below the 90°C operating setpoint).
(d) Operating Parameter: Set the base dosing rate at 20% of the manufacturer’s maximum recommended concentration for the antiscalant product, ensuring that the 5-minute pulse delivers the total mass equivalent of the standard continuous dose.
(e) Operating Parameter: Set the temperature controller’s gating threshold at 85°C; no change to the 90°C evaporator operating setpoint.
(f) Procedure: Operator manually confirms the dosing pump is online and the PWM generator is enabled at startup; no additional calibration or commissioning required beyond standard PLC programming.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
The standard practice bill includes: dosing pump (a), continuous-flow timer or valve (b), temperature controller (c), antiscalant chemical (d). The proposed bill replaces the continuous-flow timer with a PWM generator (b) and adds a temperature-gating signal (c). The hardware class is identical: the PWM generator is a standard PLC module, the dosing pump is the same catalog part, the temperature controller is existing. The operational loss is zero: the evaporator throughput and energy input are unchanged; only the dosing schedule changes. The antiscalant consumption is reduced by 50%, yielding a net cost reduction. The burden is the same-or-lower class: no new hardware beyond standard PLC modules, no process changes to the evaporator, no custom calibration. The deployment is open-loop on stated physics (thermal-peak scaling window) and rides existing instrumentation (temperature controller).

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Install the PWM-gated dosing schedule on the evaporator. Measure the antiscalant concentration in the brine loop at the 15-minute mark (during the 5-minute pulse peak) and the 45-minute mark (during the zero-dose interval) using a standard conductivity meter. Measure the scale deposition rate on the heat-transfer surface after 50 duty cycles (approx. 50 hours at 1-hour cycle) by weighing a standard surface coupon or using a standard scale-thickness gauge.
Instruments: Standard conductivity meter (existing in the plant), standard scale-thickness gauge or coupon scale (standard catalog part).
Pass/Fail Thresholds: (1) Antiscalant concentration during the pulse peak must be 3x the continuous-dosing baseline concentration (verifying the 20% base rate at 5-min pulse yields the total mass). (2) Scale deposition rate per duty cycle must be < 10% of the baseline continuous-dosing rate after 50 cycles.
Duration: 50 hours (50 duty cycles).
Kill Criterion: If the scale deposition rate does not drop by at least 50% relative to the baseline, the mechanism is invalid (the thermal-peak window is not the sole driver of scale, or the antiscalant kinetics are not nonlinear enough to benefit from pulsing).
